dabble.e: From earlier dable, equivalent to dab + -le (frequentative suffix), possibly from Middle Dutch dabbelen (“to pinch; knead; to fumble; to dabble”).

demerit.e: From Middle English demerit, demerite, from Old French desmerite (modern French démérite) and its etymon Latin dēmeritum. By surface analysis, de- + merit.

democratization.x: Autocratization is more prevalent than democratization in every region of the world.

demolition.e: From Old French demolition, from Latin dēmōlītiō (“a tearing down”). Equivalent to demolish + -ion.

demonic.e: From Latin daemonicus, from Ancient Greek δαιμονικός (daimonikós, “possessed by a demon, sent by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn), equivalent to demon + -ic.

demonstration.e: From Middle English demonstracioun, from Old French demonstration, from Latin dēmōnstrātiōnem, from dēmōnstrāre (“show or explain”), from dē- (“of or concerning”) +…

demote.x: James was demoted from branch manager to assistant manager due to his poor discipline.

demure.e: Inherited from Middle English demure, demwre, an abbreviation of Anglo-Norman de mure port (“with a mature demeanor”) (compare Old French meur from Latin mātūrus): *si il…

demystify.e: From French démystifier, or de- + mystify.

denial.x: The singer has issued a sweeping denial of all the rumors.

denim.e: From the French phrase de Nîmes (“from Nîmes”), after the French town of Nîmes, where denim fabric was originally produced.

denomination.e: From Middle English denominacioun, from Old French denominacion, from Latin dēnōminātiō. By surface analysis, denominate + -ion.
denomination.x: She follows the Ahmadiyya denomination of Islam.

denote.e: From Middle French denoter, from Latin denotare, from de- (“complete”) and notare (“to mark out”).
denote.x: The yellow blazes denote the trail.

denounce.e: From Old French denuncier, from Latin dēnūntiō (“to announce, to denounce, to threaten”), from de + nūntiō (“to announce, to report, to denounce”), from nūntius…

dense.e: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús)).

density.e: Borrowed from Middle French densité or Latin densitas. Morphologically dense + -ity.

dentist.x: Oh, you couldn't be married to a dentist. Don't be silly.

dentistry.x: A corporation may not operate a dentistry office unless all of its stockholders are licensed to practice dentistry.

denture.e: From French denture (“set of teeth”), from Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + -urus, -ura, -urum, a suffix implying a set.
denture.x: After the mouth surgery, she was fitted with a denture.

deodorant.e: From Latin de- + odorans, present participle of odorare (“to smell”), from odor (“a smell”); see odor. By surface analysis, de- + odor + -ant.

depart.e: From Old French departir, from Late Latin departiō (“to divide”), from dē- (“away from”) + partiō (“part, divide”).

departure.e: From Old French deporteure (“departure; figuratively, death”). By surface analysis, depart + -ure.

dependence.e: From Middle French dépendance. Morphologically depend + -ence.

dependency.e: From dependent + -cy or dependence + -y or depend + -ency.

dependent.e: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent, from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (“to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō…

depiction.e: From French dépiction, from Latin dēpictiō. By surface analysis, depict + -ion.

deplete.e: Borrowed from Latin dēplētus (“empty”), from depleō. First attested in 1716; originally a medical term.
deplete.x: The winter storm quickly depleted the salt supply of the county.

deplore.e: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.
deplore.x: I deplore my neighbour for having lost his job.

deployment.e: From French déploiement. Also de- + ployment.

deport.e: Borrowed from French déporter. With the meaning of "behave", from Old French deporter (“behave”), from Latin deportō, from de- + portō.
deport.x: Ask her to deport all illegals living in this town without a green card or the appropriate documents that prove their naturalized citizenship.

deportation.e: From Middle French déportation, equivalent to deport + -ation.

depose.e: Recorded since c.1300, from Middle English, from Old French deposer, from de- (“down”) + poser (“to put, place”).
depose.x: A deposed monarch may go into exile as pretender to the lost throne, hoping to be restored in a subsequent revolution.

deposition.e: From Middle English deposicion, from Old French deposicion (French déposition), from Latin depositio.

depot.e: From French dépôt, from Old French depost, from Medieval Latin dēpositum, from Latin, participle of dēpōnō, dēpōnere. Doublet of deposit.

depraved.x: You are an atrocious person! Since the day I met you I have become steadily more depraved.

depreciation.x: The accountant calculated the annual depreciation of the machinery.

depressing.x: The television news was depressing, so rather than start crying I turned it off.

depression.e: From Middle English depression, depressioun, from Old French depression, from Latin dēpressiō. Equivalent to depress + -ion.
depression.x: I used to suffer from depression, but now I'm mostly content with my life.

deprivation.x: He was suffering from deprivation of sleep.

deprive.e: From Middle English depryven, from Old French depriver, from Medieval Latin dēprīvō, from Latin dē- + prīvō.

depth.e: From Middle English depthe, from Old English *dīepþ (“depth”), from Proto-Germanic *diupiþō (“depth”), equivalent to deep + -th (abstract nominal suffix).

derby.e: From Epsom Derby horse race, named after Edward Smith-Stanley, 12th Earl of Derby. Ultimately from Derby.

derelict.x: There was a derelict ship on the island.

derisive.e: From the participle stem of Latin dērīdeō (“to deride”) + -ive.

derivation.e: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

dermatology.e: From Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”) + -logy. Analysable as dermato- + -logy.

dermis.e: From New Latin dermis, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”).

descent.e: From Middle English and Anglo-Norman descente, from Anglo-Norman descendre (“to descend”); see descend. Compare ascent, ascend. Doublet of desant.

descriptive.e: From Latin dēscriptīvus (“containing a full description”).

desecration.x: It seemed a desecration and an unhallowed thing to touch that sleeping image of the live man by my side.

deserter.e: Borrowed from Latin desertor (“deserter”), from desero (“to forsake, to abandon”); or from desert + -er.

designate.e: Borrowed from Latin dēsignātus, perfect passive participle of designō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of design.

designation.e: From Middle English designacioun, from Latin dēsignātiō, and partly (especially in sense 5) from design + -ation. By surface analysis, designate + -ion.

desirable.e: From Old French desirable. Morphologically desire + -able.

desist.e: Borrowed from Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō, from dē- + sistō (whence de-).

desolate.e: From Middle English desolat(e). See Etymology 2 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

despondent.e: From Latin dēspondēns, from the verb despondere (“to give up, to abandon”).

despot.e: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”).

despotic.e: From Ancient Greek δεσποτικός (despotikós) via French despotique, equivalent to despot + -ic.

destitute.e: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.

destitution.e: From Old French destitution, from Latin dēstitūtiō (“abandoning”), from dēstituō.

destructive.e: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.

detach.e: From Old French destachier, from the same root as attach; compare French détacher and Portuguese and Spanish destacar.

detachment.e: From French détachement. By surface analysis, detach + -ment.

detain.e: From Old French detenir. Doublet of détente. Cognate with Italian detenere, Portuguese deter, Romanian deține, and Spanish detener.

detection.e: Learned borrowing from Latin dētēctiō. By surface analysis, detect + -ion.

detector.e: Borrowed from Latin dētēctor. Equals detect + -or (agent noun forming suffix).

detention.e: Borrowed from Middle French détention, from Latin detentio, detentionem. Equivalent to detain + -tion.

deter.e: Borrowed from Latin dēterreō (“deter, discourage”), from de (“from”) + terreō (“to frighten”).

deterioration.e: Borrowed from French détérioration; morphologically deteriorate + -ion.

detritus.e: Learned borrowing from Latin dētrītus (“(that which is) rubbed away”), from dēterō (“rub away”).

deuterium.x: Heavy water is "heavy" because it contains deuterium.

devastate.e: Borrowed from Latin dēvastātus, perfect passive participle of dēvastō (“to lay waste, devastate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)).

deviate.e: From Late Latin dēviātus, perfect passive participle of dēviō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Compare French dévier.

devilish.e: From Middle English develissh, develyssh, equivalent to devil + -ish.

devious.e: 1590s, "out of the common or direct way," from Latin devius (“out of the way, remote, off the main road”), from de via, from de (“off”) (see de-) + via (“way, road”).

devise.e: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.

devoted.x: Bob and Sara are devoted to their children.

devotee.e: From devote + -ee. The narrowed meaning in sense 3 arises from the sound similarity with amputee.
devotee.x: He was a devotee of Arnold Schwarzenegger.

devotion.e: From Old French devocion, from Latin dēvōtiō, from dēvōtum + -tio, from the supine of dēvoveō (“vow, devote”); equivalent to devote + -ion.
devotion.x: Her devotion to her family was clear in everything she did.

devour.e: Inherited from Middle English devouren, from Old French devorer (Modern French dévorer), from Latin dēvorō, from vorō.

devout.x: We must be constant and devout in the worship of our God.

dewdrop.e: From Middle English deu drop, dew droppe, dewe droppe, equivalent to dew + drop.

diagnosis.x: Diagnosis is a challenging art informed by wide-ranging science.

dialysis.e: From Latin dialysis, from Ancient Greek διάλυσις (diálusis). By surface analysis, dia- + -lysis. First use appears c. 1550.

diaphanous.e: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

diarrhea.x: I looked and saw that she and her hammock were covered in diarrhea.

diaspora.x: The African diaspora caused a melding of cultures, both African cultures and Western ones, in many places.

dichotomy.x: The dichotomy between maria and highlands dominates lunar mineralogy.

dictation.e: From Late Latin dictātiō, noun of action from dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō. By surface analysis, dictate + -ion.

diligence.e: Borrowed from French diligence, from Latin diligentia.

dimple.x: The accident created a dimple in the hood of the car.

dinar.e: From Arabic دِينَار (dīnār) and Serbo-Croatian динар (also from Arabic), derived from the Latin dēnārius. Doublet of denar, denarius, denier, diner, dinero, and dinheiro.

dinghy.e: From Bengali ডিঙি (ḍiṅi), perhaps from Sanskrit द्रोण (droṇa, “wooden trough”).

dingo.e: Borrowed from Dharug dingu (“tame or domesticated dingo”).

diplomacy.e: From French diplomatie, a back-formation from diplomatique, ultimately from Latin diploma (“a letter of recommendation or authority”); see diploma.

diplomat.e: From French diplomate, a back-formation from diplomatique (“diplomatic”), ultimately from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “double-folded document”).
diplomat.x: The French diplomat negotiated the peace treaty.

diplomatic.e: From French diplomatique and its etymon New Latin diplōmaticus. By surface analysis, diplomat + -ic.
diplomatic.x: She spent thirty years working for Canada's diplomatic service.

dipper.e: From Middle English dippere; equivalent to dip + -er.

directive.e: From Middle French directif. The noun senses are from French directive (feminine form of the adjective).
directive.x: A directive management style is stronger among owners with 'lifestyle' as a business objective than among those with business/economic objectives.

directory.e: From Middle English directorie, dyrectorye, from Medieval Latin dīrēctōrium. By surface analysis, direct + -ory. Doublet of directorium.

dirham.e: From Arabic دِرْهَم (dirham), ultimately from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ). Doublet of dram, drachma, diram, dirhem, and adarme.

disadvantage.e: From Middle English disavauntage, from Old French desavantage.

disagreeable.e: Inherited from Middle English disagreable, from Middle French desagreable, from Old French desagraable (compare French désagréable).

disagreement.x: They had a bit of a disagreement about what color to paint the bedroom, but they have reached a compromise.

disappearance.x: Wireless phone technology led to the disappearance of once-common coiled cords for telephone handsets.

disappoint.e: From Middle English disapointen, disapoynten, from Middle French desapointer, desappointer (modern French désappointer).

disapproval.x: Everyone glared in disapproval at the man talking loudly on the phone.

disapprove.x: She disapproves of rap music because of its sometimes aggressive lyrics.

disarm.e: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.

disarmament.e: From disarm + -ment, modeled after armament. By surface analysis, dis + armament.

disarray.e: From Middle English disareyen (“to disarray”), from Middle French desarroyer, from Old French desareer, from des- (“dis-”) + areer (“to array”).
disarray.x: Who with fiery steeds / Oft disarray'd the foes in battle ranged.

disassemble.x: To perform the repair it was necessary to disassemble most of the mechanism.

disastrous.e: From disaster + -ous, after Middle French desastreux (modern French désastreux; from desastre (modern French désastre, “disaster”.

disavow.e: From dis- + avow, or from Old French desavouer.
disavow.x: He was charged with embezzlement, but he disavows the crime.

disband.e: Attested since the 1590s, from Middle French desbander (Modern French débander), from des- (English dis-) + bande (English band), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European…
disband.x: The president wanted to disband the scandal-plagued agency.

disburse.e: From Old French desbourser (Modern French débourser). By surface analysis, dis- + burse (“purse”).

discard.e: From dis- + card. Compare Spanish descartar.

discernible.e: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.

discharge.e: From Middle English dischargen, from Old French deschargier (“to unload”), from Late Latin discarricāre (“unload”). By surface analysis, dis- + charge.

disciplinary.e: From Medieval Latin disciplinarius, from Latin disciplina (“instruction, teaching, field of study, habit”).

disclaimer.e: Partly from Middle English discleymer, from Anglo-Norman desclamer; and partly from disclaim + -er.

discomfort.e: From Middle English discomforten, from Anglo-Norman descomforter, equivalent to dis- + comfort.

discontinue.e: From Old French descontinuer, equivalent to dis- + continue.

discontinuity.e: From Late Latin discontinuitās, from discontinuus, equivalent to dis- + continuity.

discreet.e: From Middle English discrete, from Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, from past participle of discernere. Doublet of discrete.

discrepancy.x: They found a discrepancy between the first set of test results and the second, and they're still trying to figure out why.

discrete.e: From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”). Doublet of discreet.
discrete.x: "I resign my life, but not my honour" is a discrete proposition.

discretion.e: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.
discretion.x: Bob showed great discretion despite his knowledge of the affair.

discriminate.e: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin discrīminātus, perfect passive participle of discrīminō (“to divide, separate, distinguish”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)…

discrimination.e: Learned borrowing from Latin discrīminātiō, discrīminātiōnem, the action noun to discrīminō, discrīmināre (“distinguish”). Equivalent to discriminate + -ion.

discus.e: 1656. From Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, dish, disk, and diskos.

disdain.e: From Middle English disdeynen, from Old French desdeignier (modern French dédaigner).

disgrace.e: From Middle French disgracier. Mostly displaced Modern English shand.

dishevelled.e: From earlier dishevely, from Old French deschevelé (modern French déchevelé and échevelé), from des- (“dis-”), + chevel (“hair”) (modern French cheveu).

dishonest.e: From Middle English dishoneste (“dishonourable”), from Old French deshoneste, from Latin dehonestus. Equivalent to dis- + honest. Displaced native Old English unsōþfæst.

dishonesty.e: From Middle English dishoneste (“disgrace, filth”), from Old French deshoneste, equivalent to dis- + honesty or dishonest + -y.

dishonour.e: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honour.
dishonour.x: You have brought dishonour upon the family.

dishwasher.e: From Middle English dysche wescheare, equivalent to dish + washer.

dishwater.x: This season's offerings are nothing but dishwater.

disillusionment.x: But till I am thirty, I know that my youth will triumph over everything- every disillusionment, every disgust with life.

disinfect.e: From English dis- + infect, from Middle French desinfecter.

disinfectant.e: From disinfect + -ant, borrowed from French désinfectant.

disinfection.x: In brief, after application of the speculum and disinfection of the cervix, the hysterovideoscope was introduced intracervically.

disinformation.e: Composed of dis- + information. Attested in the sense “intentional misinformation” in English from 1939.

disinherit.e: From Middle English disenheriten, equivalent to dis- + inherit.

disintegration.x: The sample exhibited an activity of three disintegrations per second.

disinterest.x: She eyed him over her martini with cool disinterest.

disinterested.e: From disinterest (“to cause to be impartial”, verb) + -ed (suffix forming past tense or past participle forms of verbs), or from dis- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + interested…

dislocation.e: From Middle English, from Old French, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dislocātiō, delocatio.

dislodge.e: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Compare French déloger. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.

disloyal.e: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman desleal, desloial, equivalent to dis- + loyal.

disloyalty.e: From Old French desloiauté (Modern French déloyauté), from des- + loiauté (“loyalty”).

dismal.e: From Middle English dismal, dismale, from Anglo-Norman dismal, from Old French (li) dis mals (“(the) bad days”), from Medieval Latin diēs malī (“bad days”).
dismal.x: Liverpool's efforts thereafter had an air of desperation as their dismal 2012 league form continued.

dismantle.e: From Middle French desmanteler, itself from des- (“dis-”), mantel (“coat”) + -er (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, dis- + mantle.

dismiss.x: The company dismissed me after less than a year.

dismount.e: From dis- + mount, probably a calque of Old French desmonter.

disobedience.e: From Middle English disobedience, dysobediaunce, from Old French desobedience. By surface analysis, dis- + obedience. Displaced native Old English unhīersumnes.

disobedient.e: From Middle English disobedient, dysobedyent, from Old French desobedient; morphologically, from dis- + obedient.

disorderly.e: From disorder + -ly (adjectival suffix) or from dis- + orderly.

disorganized.x: He is quite disorganized and has difficulty planning his day or remembering when his homework is due.

disown.x: Lord Capulet and his wife threatened to disown their daughter Juliet if she didn’t go through with marrying Count Paris.

disparage.e: From Middle English disparage (noun), disparagen (verb), from Old French desparage (noun), desparagier (verb), from des- (“dis-”) + parage (“equal rank, rank”).
disparage.x: Thou durst not thus disparage glorious arms.

disparate.x: The board of the company was decidedly disparate, with no two members from the same social or economic background.

disparity.e: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

dispatch.e: Borrowed from Spanish despachar and/or Italian dispacciare. Further etymology is uncertain. For first element des-, see dis-.
dispatch.x: Scores of foreign journalists have been dispatched to Seoul to report on the growing tensions between the two Koreas and the possibility of war.

dispel.e: From Middle English dispelen, from Latin dispellere (“to disperse; to dispel”).

dispensation.e: From Middle English dispensacioun, from Old French despensacion, from Latin dispensātiō. By surface analysis, dispens(e) + -ation.

dispenser.e: From Anglo-Norman dispensour, from Old French despenseor, from Latin dispensator. By surface analysis, dispense + -er.

disperse.e: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

dispersion.e: From disperse + -ion, from Middle English dispersioun, from Old French dispersion, from Latin dispersiō.

displacement.x: The displacement of the sun by parallax.

displeasure.e: From Old French desplaisir, equivalent to dis- + pleasure. See displease.

dispose.x: I dispose of my trash in the garbage can.

disposition.e: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō.

disproportionate.x: They faced a disproportionate share of the costs.

disprove.e: From Middle English disproven, dispreven, from Old French desprover, from des- + prover, equivalent to dis- + prove.

disqualification.x: Henry won the match due to the disqualification of his opponent.

disregard.x: The government's blithe disregard for the needs of disabled people is outrageous.

disrobe.e: From dis- + robe. Compare Old French desrober in the same sense.

disrupt.e: Borrowed from Latin disruptus, from disrumpo, commonly dirumpo (“to break or burst asunder”), from dis-, di- (“apart, asunder”) + rumpo (“to break”).

disruption.e: From Latin disruptionem, from disrumpere. By surface analysis, disrupt + -ion.
disruption.x: The network created a disruption in the show when they broke in with a newscast.

disruptive.e: From disrupt + -ive. In the business sense popularized by Clayton Christensen and Joseph Bower, see 1995 citation.
disruptive.x: Children who exhibit disruptive behaviour may be expelled from school.

dissatisfaction.x: Job dissatisfaction results in high turnover.

dissect.e: Borrowed from Latin dissectus past participle of dissecare (“to cut asunder, cut up”), from dis- (“asunder”) + secare (“to cut”); see section.
dissect.x: She was the first person in her class to properly dissect the sheep heart.

dissection.e: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

disseminate.x: The values of the human rights movement have disseminated throughout the world.

dissension.e: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

dissertation.x: She spent three years writing her doctoral dissertation.

disservice.x: One renders young people a disservice by heaping unearned rewards on them.

dissident.e: From Latin dissidēns, present participle of dissideō (“to sit apart; to disagree”), from dis- (“asunder, apart, in two”) + sedeō (“to sit”).
dissident.x: I once more find myself a dissident, and a dissident in a very small minority.

dissipate.e: The verb is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765.
dissipate.x: August 1773, James Cook, journal entry I soon dissipated his fears.

dissipation.e: From Middle English dissipacion, dissipacioun, from Late Latin dissipātiō. Morphologically dissipate + -ion.
dissipation.x: He neither wept nor prayed; he cursed and defied: execrated God and man, and gave himself up to reckless dissipation.

dissociation.e: Borrowed from French dissociation, from Latin dissociātiō(n).

dissolution.e: From Middle English dissolucioun, from Old French dissolucion, from Latin dissolūtiō (“a dissolving, destroying, breaking up, dissolution”).
dissolution.x: The whole fabric dries up, or becomes putrid; and, in both cases, sooner or later, tends to a dissolution.

dissolve.e: Recorded since c. 1374 (displacing Old English toliesan) as Middle English dissolven, from Latin dissolvere (“to loosen up, break apart”) but with the sense from…
dissolve.x: The ruling party or coalition sometimes dissolves parliament early when the polls are favorable, hoping to reconvene with a larger majority.

dissonance.e: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.

dissuade.e: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to…
dissuade.x: Jane dissuaded Martha from committing suicide.

distil.e: From Late Middle English distillen (“to fall, flow, or shed in drops, drop, trickle; to shed drops; to fill (the eyes) with tears.

distillation.e: From Middle English distillacioun, from Anglo-Norman distillacioun, from Latin distīllātiōnem, accusative of distīllātiō.
distillation.x: to be stopped in, like a strong distillation, with stinking / clothes that fretted in their own grease.

distinct.e: From Middle English distincte, past participle of distincten (“to distinguish, discern”), from Old French destincter, from Latin distinctus, past participle of…

distinction.e: From Middle English distinccioun, from Old French distinction (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin distinctiōnem, action noun of distinguō (“separate…

distinctive.e: From Latin distinctus, perfect passive participle of distinguere (to push apart, to divide; see distinct) + -ive (forming adjectives signifying relation or tendency to).

distinctly.x: I distinctly remember the voice of my deceased grandmother.

distinguish.e: From Middle English distingwen, from Old French distinguer, from Latin distinguere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from di-…
distinguish.x: The soldier distinguished himself in combat and received a medal.

distinguished.x: The lecture was attended by many distinguished mathematicians.

distort.e: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).
distort.x: In their articles, journalists sometimes distort the truth.

distortion.e: Borrowed from Latin distortio, distortionis, from distortus.
distortion.x: The story he told was a bit of a distortion.

distract.e: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).
distract.x: The crowd was distracted by a helicopter hovering over the stadium when the only goal of the game was scored.

distraction.e: Borrowed from Middle French distraction, from Latin distractio. Equivalent to distract + -ion.
distraction.x: Poking one's eye is a good distraction from a hurting toe.

distraught.e: From Middle English distraught, blend of distract (“distracted”) and straught (“stretched, distraught”), past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”).
distraught.x: His distraught widow cried for days, feeling very alone.

distress.e: The verb is from Middle English distressen, from Old French destrecier (“to restrain, constrain, put in straits, afflict, distress”); compare French détresse.
distress.x: If he were not paid, he would straight go and take a distress of goods and cattle.

distressed.x: She is distressed because she can't find her keys.

distribute.e: PIE word *tréyes From Latin distributus, past participle of distribuere (“to divide, distribute”), from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to give, impart”); see tribute.
distribute.x: He distributed the bread amongst his followers.

distribution.e: From Old French distribution, from Latin distributio, from distribuere (“to distribute”), itself from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to assign, allot”) (from tribus).

distributor.x: The recall said that the distributors — Walmart, CVS and AACE Pharmaceuticals — will be arranging the return of all the affected products.

disturbance.e: From Middle English disturbaunce, from Old French destorbance, destourbance, from destourber (“disturb”), from Latin disturbō. By surface analysis, disturb + -ance.
disturbance.x: That guy causes a lot of trouble, you know, he’s such a disturbance.

ditto.e: First attested in 1625. From regional Italian ditto, variant of detto, past participle of dire (“to say”), from Latin dīcō (“to say, to speak”).

diurnal.e: From Latin diurnālis, from diēs (“day”). Doublet of journal.
diurnal.x: However, in general, lizards are more diurnal than rattlers, which may be one of the reasons why young rattlers are more diurnal than adults.

divan.e: Borrowed from French, from Ottoman Turkish دیوان (divan), from Classical Persian دیوان (dēwān), from Middle Persian d(p)ywʾn' (dēwān, “archive, collected writings”), from…

diver.x: A passerby noticed the man's body protruding from the water at about 9 p.m. and Boston and Metropolitan police divers were called to the scene.

diverge.e: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).
diverge.x: Both stories start out the same way, but they diverge halfway through.

divergence.x: An angle is made by the divergence of straight lines.

divergent.e: From Latin dis- (“apart”) + vergere (“to turn”) + the adjectival suffix -ent.
divergent.x: Four zebras stood despondent facing divergent directions like an old European film or a '90s band photo.

diverse.e: PIE word *dwóh₁ The adjective is derived from Middle English divers, diverse (“different, divergent”), from Anglo-Norman divers, Anglo-Norman divers, and Old French…
diverse.x: Eloquence is a great and diverse thing.

diversification.e: From Medieval Latin diversificatiō, from diversificātus, past participle of diversificō (“diversify”), from Latin diversus (“turned in different ways”) + faciō (“make…

diversify.e: Borrowed from Middle French diversifier, equivalent to diverse + -ify.

diversion.e: From Middle English diversion, dyversioun, from Medieval Latin diversiō, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.

diversity.e: From Middle English diversite, from Old French diversité, from Latin dīversitās, equivalent to diverse + -ity. Displaced native Old English mislīcnes.
diversity.x: In much she reminded me constantly of my own lost child; in other ways she attracted me by her diversity.

divert.e: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

diverticulum.e: From Latin dīverticulum, alternative form of dēverticulum (“byroad; deviation”), from dēvertō (“turn away, turn aside”).

divide.x: Words divide us; Wiktionary unites us.

dividend.e: From Middle French dividende, from Latin dīvidendum (“thing to be divided”), future passive participle of dīvidō (“to divide”), by surface analysis, divide + -end.

divination.e: From Old French divination, from Latin divinatio.

divinity.e: From Old French divinité, from Latin divinitas. Composed of divine + -ity. Displaced native Old English godcundnes.
divinity.x: They say there is divinity in odd numbers.

divisible.e: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English divisible, from Old French, from Late Latin divisibilis, from the verb Latin divido.
divisible.x: Just as 12 is divisible by 3, so is 48 divisible by 12.

divorcee.e: Borrowed from French divorcée, equivalent to divorce + -ee.

divulge.e: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).
divulge.x: I will never divulge that secret to anyone.

dizzy.e: From Middle English dysy, desy, dusi, from Old English dysiġ (“stupid, foolish”), from Proto-West Germanic *dusīg (“stunned; dazed”).

docile.x: Such literature may well be anathema to those, who are too docile and petty for their own good.

docking.e: From Middle English dockyng. By surface analysis, dock + -ing.

dockworker.x: The East Coast dockworkers understand what’s happening around the world.

doctoral.e: From doctor + -al, probably modelled on Latin doctorālis.

doctrinal.e: The noun form was from French doctrinal; the adjective form was perhaps from Late Latin doctrīnālis, from doctrīna.

doctrine.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.
doctrine.x: The Incarnation is a basic doctrine of Christianity.

documentary.x: Such sequences draw attention to the affective appeals that environmental documentary typically makes, precisely by absenting those appeals.

dodecahedron.e: From Ancient Greek δωδεκάεδρον (dōdekáedron). Equivalent to dodeca- + -hedron.
dodecahedron.x: It took me two years, but by the time I was 12 I could imagine the fifth four-dimensional polytope, which is made up of 120 dodecahedrons.

dodge.e: Likely from dialectal dodge, dod, dodd (“to jog, trudge along, totter", also "to jerk, jig”), of uncertain origin.
dodge.x: He dodged traffic crossing the street.

dogfish.e: From dog + fish. Compare Greek σκυλόψαρο (skylópsaro, “dogfish”), Latin canicula (“dogfish”, literally “little dog”), Italian pescecane (“dogfish”), French chien de mer…

dogged.e: From Middle English dogged, doggid, doggyd (“characteristics similar to that of a dog”), equivalent to dog + -ed.
dogged.x: Still, the dogged obstinacy of his race held him to the pace he had set, and would hold him till he dropped in his tracks.

doggy.x: That's such a cute little doggy, Keira!

dogma.e: From Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”).
dogma.x: If he has a dogma, i.e. a scientifico-philosophical theory, then he is not any sort of Skeptic, not even an urbane Skeptic.

dogmatism.e: From French dogmatisme, from Ecclesiastical Latin dogmatismus.

dogwood.e: From dag + wood, from dag (“a sharp object”).

doily.e: From Doiley, the name of a 17th-century London draper. The surname is Anglo-Norman, from d'Œuilly, name of several places in Calvados, from Old French oeil (“eye”).

dolma.e: From Greek ντολμάς (ntolmás) or its etymon, Turkish dolma, from Ottoman Turkish طولمه (dolma), from طولمق (dolmak, “to get full, be filled”).

domain.x: Dealing with complaints isn't really my domain: get in touch with customer services.

domicile.e: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.

dominant.x: His story was a fable you told dominants in training to stress the importance of comprehending the depths of your submissive's needs.

dominate.e: Borrowed from Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“to rule, have dominion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dominus (“lord, master”) + -or…

domination.e: From Middle English domynacion, from Old French dominacion, from Latin dominātiō (“rule, dominion”), from dominor (“domineer; rule”); see dominate.
domination.x: First, relations of power and domination have been and continue to be significantly constitutive of social relations in modern societies.

dominion.e: From Middle English dominion, from Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium (“lordship, right of ownership”), from dominus (“lord”), from domus (“house”).
dominion.x: To choose between dominion or slavery.

domino.e: 1801, borrowed from French domino (1771), originally the term for a hooded garment, itself from Medieval Latin domino, oblique case of dominus (“lord, master”).
domino.x: Then he hunted for the black carnival domino, supposing that it was the appropriate thing for a penitent to wear.

donation.e: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”).
donation.x: They were collecting donations for the elderly at Christmas.

donkey.e: The origin is uncertain. Originally a slang term from the late eighteenth century.

donor.e: From Middle English donoure, donour; from Anglo-Norman donour, from Old French doneur (See French donneur).
donor.x: The charity raised $2,000 from various donors.

doomsday.e: From Middle English domes + dai, from Old English dom (“judgment”) + dæg (“day”). Equivalent to doom + -s- + day. Compare Old Norse dómsdagr (“judgement day, doomsday”).

doormat.x: Wipe your shoes on the doormat before you start plodding around in the house.

doorstep.x: Ailie was standing by the doorstep as he came down the road, and her heart stood still with joy.

doorway.x: I stood by the doorway to watch her go.

dopamine.e: From DOPA (“dihydroxyphenylalanine”) + -amine. Etymologically unrelated to dope.

doppelganger.e: Borrowed from German Doppelgänger (“ghostly spirit”, literally “double-walker”).
doppelganger.x: The uncanniness provoked by doppelgangers is particularly acute because the thing that becomes unfamiliar is you.

dormant.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin dormiēns, present participle of dormiō (“to sleep”).
dormant.x: Grass goes dormant during the winter, waiting for spring before it grows again.

dormer.e: From Middle French dormoir (“sleeping room”), from dormir (“to sleep”).

dormitory.e: From Middle English dormitory, dormytory, dormytorye, borrowed from Latin dormītōrium (“a sleeping-room”), from dormiō (“to sleep”). Doublet of dormitorium and dorter.

dormouse.e: From Middle English dormowse, of uncertain origin. Possibly from a dialectal *dor-, from Old Norse dár (“benumbed”) + mous (“mouse”). More at doze, mouse.

dorsal.e: From Late Middle English dorsal/dorsale, borrowing from Medieval Latin dorsālis (“of or relating to the back”), from dorsum (“the back”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival…

dosage.x: Why did he give you only a single 500 mg dose? The correct dosage of this antibiotic is one 500 mg tablet twice a day for 10 days.

dotage.e: From Middle English dotage, from doten (“to dote”) + -age; equivalent to dote + -age.
dotage.x: No leſs are they out of the way in Philoſophy, peſtring their heads with the ſapleſs dotages of old Paris and Salamanca.

doublet.e: From Middle English doublet, a borrowing from Old French doublet, from double, duble, doble + -et. Equivalent to double + -et (diminutive suffix).

doubtful.e: From Middle English doutfull, douteful, equivalent to doubt + -ful.
doubtful.x: The pupils of her great eyes were large in the doubtful lamplight, swallowing their green fires in deep pools of mystery and darkness.

douche.e: Borrowed from French douche (“shower”), from Italian doccia (“shower”).
douche.x: In the bathroom, they immersed him in a tub of warm water, and then pulled him out and put him under a cold douche.

doughnut.x: One American student sought my help to take the work further in his school science project, in which he studied how doughnuts differ from cookies.

dovetail.e: The noun is derived from dove + tail. The verb is derived from the noun.
dovetail.x: With a warding file cut a dovetail on each of the ends to be joined, as shown by Fig. 1.

dowager.e: From Middle French douagere, douagiere, from douage (“dower”), from the verb douer (“to endow”), from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”).
dowager.x: A reclusive dowager owned the pastures across the river, and her farmhands ran beef cattle on them.

downcast.e: The adjective is derived from Middle English doun-casten, *adoun-casten (“(adjective) cast down, dejected; (verb) to break down (something); to overcome (someone).
downcast.x: His fine and lovely eyes were now lighted up with indignation, now subdued to downcast sorrow and quenched in infinite wretchedness.

downfall.e: From down- + fall. In this spelling, from 16th century; spelled as two words from 13th century.
downfall.x: Many economic and political reasons led to the downfall of the Roman Empire.

downplay.e: Synthetic form of the phrase play down. By surface analysis, down- + play.

downpour.e: From down- + pour. Compare typologically Czech liják, Polish ulewa, Slovene naliv, Russian ли́вень (lívenʹ) (akin to лить (litʹ)).
downpour.x: It started to downpour, so Billy and I made our way back to our house, with Scotty following—or so I thought.

downstream.x: Input validation is downstream of input entry in the runtime process.

downtime.e: From down (“out of order; out of service; inoperable”) + time.
downtime.x: I’ve been working all weekend. I need some downtime.

downtrodden.e: From Middle English *dountroden, past participle of Middle English dountreden (“to tread down, trample”), equivalent to down- + trodden.

downward.x: His position in society moved ever downward.

downy.x: The chick's downy coat of feathers formed almost immediately to keep it warm.

dowry.e: From Middle English dowarye, dowerie, from Anglo-Norman dowarie, douarie, from Old French douaire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dower.

drachma.e: Learned borrowing from Latin drachma and its etymon Doric Greek δρᾰχμᾱ́ (drăkhmā́). Doublet of dram, diram, dirham, dirhem, adarme, and dam.

draconian.e: From Latin Dracō (stem Dracōn-) + -ian, from Ancient Greek Δράκων (Drákōn), after the Athenian lawmaker Draco, known for making harsh laws. See δράκων (drákōn, “dragon”).

drainpipe.x: She's in a drainpipe--right there," I said, pointing toward the hole in the side of the ditch.

drape.x: The herringbone-twill sample is soft and smooth, with an easy drape that allows the fabric to move beautifully.

drapery.e: From Middle English draperie, from Old French draperie, from drap (“drape, sheet, large cloth”), ultimately of Germanic origin.

draught.e: From Middle English draught, draght, draȝt, from Old English *dreaht, *dræht (related to dragan (“to draw, drag”)), from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz, noun form of *draganą.

drawback.x: Poor fuel economy is a common drawback among larger vehicles.

drawbridge.e: Inherited from Middle English drawebrigge; by surface analysis, draw + bridge.

dreadful.e: From Middle English dredful, dredfull, dredeful (also dreful). By surface analysis, dread + -ful.

dreadnought.x: Herbert steering the dreadnought limousine through the night, black cap on his black head.

dreamer.e: From Middle English dremer, dremere, dremare, equivalent to dream + -er.

dreamlike.x: Her kiss sent me into a dreamlike state of bliss.

dreary.x: It had rained for three days straight, and the dreary weather dragged the townspeople's spirits down.

dredge.e: From Scots dreg-boat, dreg-bot (from Old English *dreċġ); or alternatively from Middle Dutch dregghe (“drag-net”), probably ultimately from the same root as drag.

dregs.x: I sat through the dregs of a long hectic evening.

drenched.x: The storm's so bad that if you step outside for 20 seconds, you get drenched.

dressage.x: I'm competing in two dressages and a jumping show this weekend.

dresser.e: From Middle English dressure, dressor, dressour, a borrowing from Old French drecëur, drecëure, from the verb dresser.

dribble.x: Denny slid over a couple of steps and swung feebly at it. The ball hit the wooden frame of his racket and dribbled into the net.

driftwood.x: Every wave on the Atlantic was like a dead seagull dragging its driftwood artillery from horizon to horizon.

drinkable.e: From Middle English drinkable, drynkeable, equivalent to drink + -able.

drinker.e: From Middle English drinkere, drynkere, from Old English drincere (“drinker”), from Proto-Germanic *drinkārijaz (“drinker”), equivalent to drink + -er.

drivel.e: From Middle English dravel, dribil, a deverbal from drevelen, drivelen (Etymology 2).

driveway.x: The design originally called for a 1-lane-wide driveway leading from the street to the parking area.

drizzle.e: Perhaps a back-formation from dryseling, a dissimilated variant of Middle English drysning (“a falling of dew”), from Northumbrian Old English drysnan (“to extinguish”)…

dropper.x: The dropper left the suitcase with the bomb next to the garbage can.

drought.e: From Middle English droughte, droghte, drouȝte, from Old English drūgaþ. Cognate with Dutch droogte, Low German Dröögde.

drowning.x: It's dangerous to swim in that river — there were three drownings there last year.

drumstick.x: She could imagine the taste of the tender drumstick seeds on her tongue.

dryad.e: From Old French driade (“wood nymph”), from Latin Dryas, Dryadis, from Ancient Greek Δρυάς (Druás, “dryad”), from δρῦς (drûs, “oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *derew(o)-…
dryad.x: No Dryads sought to avert the fate of their kindred trees - no Nereides sported on the waves.

dryer.e: From Middle English driere, dreyere (“one who dries”), equivalent to dry + -er (agent noun suffix).

dryness.e: Inherited from Middle English dryenesse, drynesse; equivalent to dry + -ness.

drywall.x: Selenite is calcium sulfate, the same chemical substance (gypsum) from which drywall is made. In other words, this is crystal drywall.

dubious.e: From Latin dubius; like doubt, from Latin duo (cognate to English two), implying “two alternatives” (yes or no, true or false, etc.).

duchy.e: From Middle English duche, from Anglo-Norman duché, from Old French duc, or from Medieval Latin ducātus, from Latin dux. Doublet of ducat and dogate.

duckling.e: From Middle English dokeling, dukling, dookelynge (“duckling”), equivalent to duck + -ling.

duckweed.e: From duck + weed. Supposedly so-named for often being consumed by ducks and other waterfowl. Compare Middle English dokemete (“duckweed”, literally “duck-food”).

dugong.x: “What are those things that aren’t seals? Much worse than seals. Big, blubbery things. Dugongs.”

dumbbell.e: From dumb (“silent”) + bell (“a resonating instrument”). The term "dumbbell" originated in 16th-century England to describe silent exercise apparatus used in practicing…
dumbbell.x: He was exercising with the dumbbells in gym class today.

dumpling.e: A folk word, first attested in c. 1600s, apparently from a Norfolk (East Anglian) dialect, of uncertain origin: * perhaps from some Low German word (compare dümpeln…

dumpster.e: Genericized brand name, from blend of dump + Dempster. The original brand (and some associated things) are no longer trademarked, because the three trademarks involved…

dunce.e: 1530, named after John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308). Scotus was ironically a well-known Scottish thinker.
dunce.x: When a true genius appears in the world you may know him by this sign; that the dunces are all in confederacy against him.

dungarees.e: From dungaree + -s, from Hindi डूंगरी (ḍūṅgrī, “coarse calico”), from the name of a village.
dungarees.x: Helen donned a pair of faded dungarees and grabbed her knapsack before rushing off to school.

dungeon.e: From Middle English dongeoun (“keep of a castle; dungeon; abyss, cave, den; whirlpool”), from Anglo-Norman donjun (“keep of a castle; keep used as a prison.
dungeon.x: Year after year he lay patiently in a dungeon.

duodenum.e: From Medieval Latin duodēnum digitōrum (“space of twelve digits”) in reference to its length, from duodēnī (“twelve each”) + digitōrum, genitive plural of digitus…
duodenum.x: Duodenums were dissected out, fixed and photographed.

duplication.e: From Middle English duplicacioun, from Middle French duplication, from Late Latin duplicātiō, duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō. Morphologically duplicate + -ion.
duplication.x: Another argument for closing Woodhead was simply one of route duplication, and this was the main reason put forward by BR at the time.

duplicitous.x: “(chuckles) That duplicitous genius. She's betraying me! She's probably already on Plymeria, subjugating its feeble populace. -Quick, to the shuttle.”

duplicity.e: From Latin duplicare (double). Equivalent to duplex + -ity.

durability.e: From Middle English durabilite, from Old French durabilité, from Latin dūrābilitās (“durability”). Corresponding to durable + -ity.

durable.e: From Middle English durable, from Old French durable, from Latin dūrābilis (“lasting, permanent”), from dūrō (“harden, make hard”).
durable.x: I forged a durable relationship with my seatmate.

duration.x: The duration of the flight will be about 2 hours 45 minutes.

duress.e: Inherited from Middle English duresse, from Old French duresse, from Latin dūritia (“hardness”), from dūrus (“hard”).
duress.x: It is unclear when it was filmed and if she was under duress during filming.

durian.e: From Malay durian, ultimately from Proto-Austronesian *duʀi (“thorn”). Doublet of iwi, from Māori.
durian.x: Old women crouched over bags of Siamese rice, skeps of red and green peppers, purple egg-plants, bristly rambutans, pineapples, durians.

duster.x: Many wildcatters dug dry wells, or “dusters,” and scurried away in despair.

dusty.e: From Middle English dusty, dusti, from Old English dūstiġ, dystiġ, dȳstiġ (“dusty”), equivalent to dust + -y.
dusty.x: On a cold morning in Abilene, Texas, a column of 18-wheelers crawls down bumpy, waterlogged roads, past cattle grazing on dusty shrubs.

dwarfism.x: Studies of disproportionate dwarfisms in animals have revealed the importance of core proteins an sulfation in the development of cartilage.

dwell.x: I am fully resolved to go dwell in another house.

dwelling.e: From Middle English dwellynge, dwellyng (“delay, continuance, abode”), equivalent to dwell + -ing. More at dwell.
dwelling.x: The old house served as a dwelling for Albert.

dwindle.e: Frequentative form of dwine, from Middle English dwynen, from Old English dwīnan (“to waste away”), from Proto-West Germanic *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną.
dwindle.x: Their supplies began to dwindle after a week.

dynamic.x: The environment is dynamic, changing with the years and the seasons.

dynamics.x: The changing dynamics in international politics led to such an outcome.

dynamo.e: A shortening of dynamo-electric machine. The element dynamo- is ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”).
dynamo.x: "As usual, it isn't telling the truth about it or you. But your body is. I can feel its vitality like the pulse of a dynamo."

dynastic.e: From Ancient Greek δυναστικός (dunastikós). By surface analysis, dynasty + -ic.

dynasty.e: Borrowed from Middle French dynastie, from Late Latin dynastia, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).
dynasty.x: A dynasty is nothing but the successful orchestration of treachery.

dysfunctional.x: Live dysfunctional, likely die dysfunctional; live eufunctional, likely die eufunctional.

dyslexia.e: Learned borrowing from French dyslexie and/or German Dyslexie, coined by German ophthalmologist Rudolf Berlin in 1887, from dys- + lexis + -ia, from Ancient Greek δυσ-…

dysphoria.e: From Ancient Greek δυσφορία (dusphoría, “excessive pain”), from δύσφορος (dúsphoros, “grievous”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + φέρω (phérō, “I bear, carry”).
dysphoria.x: Chronic dysphoria can be secondary to a debilitating medical illness, a psychiatric disorder, or both (Akiskal, 1983).

dyspnea.e: Variant spelling of dyspnoea, a learned borrowing from Latin dyspnoea (“difficulty breathing”), from Ancient Greek δῠ́σπνοιᾰ (dŭ́spnoiă, “difficulty breathing, shortness…

dystopia.e: From dys- + -topia, as if from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”) + -ία (-ía), based on utopia being reinterpreted as eu-topia.
dystopia.x: The patient suffers from adrenal dystopia.

dystopian.x: The whole city is immersed in a dystopian-looking smog: urban streets in sepia, emptier than usual, bathed in an eerie quiet.

dystrophy.e: From dys- + -trophy, literally “bad growth”, as in the opposite of growth.
